workedExamples.label: worked example
workedExamples.title: Worked example — subnetting drill (not a scored item)
workedExamples.body: Host 192.168.10.42/26 needs to reach 192.168.10.100. A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192, so each subnet holds 64 addresses: .0–.63, .64–.127, .128–.191, .192–.255. The host's network is 192.168.10.0/26 (.0–.63) and the destination .100 sits in 192.168.10.64/26. The two addresses are on different subnets, so the host sends the packet to its default gateway rather than ARPing for .100. If the mask had been /24, both addresses would share one subnet and the host would ARP directly. The drill is: write the block size, find each network, then apply the local-vs-remote rule from N1. Interactive subnetting exercises are a declared gap (REQ-NP-04) — this walkthrough is labeled, not scored, and not a fake interactive lab.

workedExamples.label: worked example
workedExamples.title: Worked example — routing protocols at recognition level (not a scored item)
workedExamples.body: A small office has one router and a default route to the ISP. Nothing fancy is required: a static default gateway is enough. When a second router and multiple paths appear, a routing protocol (for example OSPF inside an organization, or BGP between organizations) is how routers exchange what they know about reachable networks instead of a human typing every static route. Worked reading: a diagram shows Router A and Router B both advertising 10.20.0.0/16. If A's link fails and the protocol withdraws the route, traffic shifts to B. If the protocol does not converge, traffic black-holes. For the October 23 demo, know that routing protocols are how paths are learned and healed; detailed metric calculation and neighbor state machines are a declared gap filled by this labeled example (REQ-NP-04).

workedExamples.label: worked example
workedExamples.title: Worked example — wireless design walk-through (not a scored item)
workedExamples.body: An office wants guest Wi-Fi and staff Wi-Fi on the same floor. Worked decisions, in order: (1) placement — APs spread for coverage with overlap, not stacked in a closet; (2) channels — non-overlapping channels on neighbors (2.4 GHz 1/6/11, or 5 GHz planning) so APs do not fight; (3) security — staff on WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise or a strong PSK, guests on an isolated VLAN with no route to internal servers; (4) power — just enough to cover the floor without spilling into the parking lot. The result is not "more power and one SSID." Full site survey tooling and RF heat maps are a declared gap (REQ-NP-04); this walkthrough is labeled and not interactive.

workedExamples.label: worked example
workedExamples.title: Worked example — packet analysis reading (not a scored item)
workedExamples.body: A capture shows: TCP SYN from client 10.1.20.55:50000 to server 10.1.20.10:443, then no SYN-ACK, repeated SYNs, and the client eventually resets. Worked reading: the client is willing and the path at Layer 3 carried the SYN (we see it addressed), but the service on 443 did not answer — either the port is closed/filtered, the host is unreachable at Layer 4, or something in between is dropping the session. Compare with a capture of the same client to port 22 where SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK completes: the network path works, so the fault is specific to the HTTPS service. No packet-analysis homework ships in this preview; this labeled example stands in until a capture lab exists (REQ-NP-04).
